summary: For ages 5–7: understand that indigenous peoples such as the Yanomami are living communities in the Amazon today who have lived in the rainforest for thousands of years, building homes from forest materials, finding food by hunting, fishing and gathering, and holding deep, expert knowledge of the forest's plants and animals. Teaching uses present tense, correct people-names, and foregrounds respect — avoiding 'primitive', generic 'tribe', and costume/spectacle framing. Core activities anchor each part of life (home, food, medicine) to the forest as provider; a respectful first-person meeting and a dignified matching check are offered as alternatives with distinct purposes rather than ranked as superior.
misconceptions: 'Indigenous peoples lived long ago / don't exist any more' — in fact the Yanomami and many others live in rainforests today.
'They are primitive or don't know much' — the opposite: they hold extremely deep, expert knowledge of the forest.
'Everyone lives in houses and shops like mine' — not realising people can meet all their needs directly from the forest.
'It's a costume/dressing-up thing' — treating a living culture as a fancy-dress theme rather than real people's lives.

activities.title: Explore a Yanomami home scene: where does everything come from?
steps: Look at a warm, accurate picture of Yanomami life in the Amazon today, centred on a great circular shabono (communal round home) in its forest setting.
Find the Yanomami on a simple map of the Amazon, noting this is a real place where they live today.
Point to the curved roof and answer the question 'What is this home made from?' — then reveal it is built from forest wood and woven palm leaves, by people who know exactly which trees to use.
Point to the river and describe what the family is doing (fishing), point to someone setting off to hunt in the forest, then point to a basket and find gathered fruits and nuts.
Point to a leafy plant and learn it is used as medicine, with knowledge of forest medicines passed down over many generations.
Say out loud, for each thing you found, which need it meets — home, food or medicine — and that it comes from the forest.
Practise using the people's own name: 'the Yanomami live in the Amazon today.'
activities.insight: Many things the Yanomami need — materials for their homes, food and medicine — come from the forest they understand so deeply, and these are real people living in the world right now whose knowledge deserves respect, not a story from long ago.

activities.title: Meet someone who lives in the rainforest
steps: Have a warm, respectful spoken exchange with a (sensitively, in-role) Yanomami child or elder about daily life: where they sleep, what they eat, how they find medicine.
Ask one question of your own, such as 'How did you learn which plants help when someone is sick?'
Listen to the reply and say back one thing you learned about how the forest provides for them.
Talk about why it would be rude to treat their way of living as 'strange' or as dressing-up, and what is admirable about their forest knowledge.
activities.insight: Indigenous peoples are real people living today with daily lives and expert knowledge learned over many generations — a person to meet and admire, not an exotic spectacle.

activities.title: Match the need to what the forest provides
steps: Sort or match cards: place 'home' with wood and woven palm leaves; place 'food' with the river (fish) and the basket (fruit and nuts); place 'medicine' with the leafy plant.
For each match, say the forest→need link aloud: 'The forest gives wood and leaves, so they can build a home.'
Add, where you can, that they have known these plants and places for a very long time — thousands of years.
activities.insight: Each basic need — shelter, food, medicine — can be met from the rainforest the Yanomami know well.

checkQuestion: Do indigenous rainforest peoples like the Yanomami only exist in stories from long ago, or are they real people living today? Tell me which, and then tell me WHY they know the forest so well.
checkAnswer: They are real people living today (not just from long ago). Peoples like the Yanomami have lived in the rainforest for thousands of years and still do, and they know it deeply because they use its plants, animals and materials every day for food, shelter and medicine — knowledge passed down over many generations.
